content: Protons are subatomic particles classified as spin-1/2 fermions, composed of three quarks—specifically, two up quarks and one down quark. These quarks are bound together by the strong nuclear force, which is mediated by gluons. Protons, along with neutrons, are collectively referred to as nucleons. Within atomic nuclei, nucleons are held together by the nuclear force. The simplest atomic nucleus, that of the most common isotope of hydrogen, consists of a single proton without any neutrons. In contrast, the nuclei of heavier hydrogen isotopes, such as deuterium and tritium, contain both protons and neutrons. All other atomic nuclei are composed of two or more protons and varying numbers of neutrons. The number of protons in a nucleus determines the chemical properties of the atom and defines the chemical element it represents. The specific isotope of an element is determined by the combined number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. The proton’s antiparticle is the antiproton, which was discovered in 1955 by Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain. This discovery earned them the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. The properties of protons and antiprotons are subject to stringent tests under the framework of CPT symmetry, which imposes strict constraints on the relative characteristics of particles and their corresponding antiparticles. For instance, the charges of the proton and antiproton must sum to exactly zero, a condition that has been experimentally verified to a precision of one part in 10^8. Similarly, the equality of their masses has been tested to better than one part in 10^8. By confining antiprotons in a Penning trap, the charge-to-mass ratio of protons and antiprotons has been measured with a precision of one part in 9 × 10^11. The magnetic moment of the antiproton has also been measured with an error margin of 8 × 10^-3 nuclear Bohr magnetons and is found to be equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to that of the proton. Protons are particularly well-suited for use in high-energy particle physics experiments due to their stability and relatively large mass compared to electrons. They are extensively utilized in particle colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN and the Tevatron at Fermilab. Protons also constitute the majority of cosmic rays that interact with the Earth's atmosphere. However, studying high-energy proton collisions is more complex than studying electron collisions because of the composite nature of protons. Understanding the intricate details of proton structure requires the application of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the interactions of quarks and gluons. Historically, the discovery of the proton is attributed to Ernest Rutherford. In 1918, Rutherford observed that when alpha particles were directed into nitrogen gas, his scintillation detectors detected the presence of hydrogen nuclei. He deduced that these hydrogen nuclei must have originated from the nitrogen atoms, leading to the conclusion that nitrogen contains hydrogen nuclei. Rutherford proposed that the hydrogen nucleus, known to have an atomic number of 1, was an elementary particle. Prior to Rutherford’s work, Eugene Goldstein had observed canal rays, which were composed of positively charged ions. Goldstein hypothesized the existence of a positively charged particle within the atom to balance the negative charge of the electron, as the atom is electrically neutral. He studied canal rays, which moved in the opposite direction to the electron flow in cathode ray tubes. These positively charged particles were created when electrons were stripped from atoms within the tube, causing the remaining particles to move toward the cathode. Goldstein initially believed he had discovered the proton, but further investigation revealed that the particles he observed were ions, not protons. Despite his efforts, Goldstein’s work was largely overlooked. In terms of their fundamental composition, protons are baryons, a category of particles made up of three quarks. The strong force, mediated by gluons, binds the quarks together within the proton. Protons and neutrons, as nucleons, can be bound together by the nuclear force to form atomic nuclei. The number of protons in a nucleus determines the element, while the total number of protons and neutrons defines the isotope of that element. The proton’s mass is approximately 1.6726 × 10^-27 kilograms, or about 1836 times the mass of an electron. In summary, protons are essential components of atomic nuclei, playing a critical role in defining the chemical and physical properties of matter. Their stability, interactions, and fundamental properties make them a cornerstone of both atomic theory and high-energy physics.
